title: light passed hand to hand
hook: a flame on a plate, moved in circles, then carried around the room

segments.voice: Yesterday: japa. Your line was count what you want to keep. Did you count a few on your fingers? Two weeks today. Day fourteen.
screen: `COUNT WHAT YOU WANT TO KEEP.` → `TWO WEEKS.`

segments.voice: Evening at a temple. Or the steps down to a river, as dusk comes in. Or a living room, when the lamp comes out. A small flame sits on a metal plate, and someone moves it in slow circles in front of the shrine. A bell rings. People sing. Then the plate is carried around the room, and one by one, people pass their hands over the flame and bring their palms to their eyes and forehead. It takes a few minutes, start to finish. Today's word is that flame, and what happens when it leaves the shrine.
screen: `A FLAME ON A PLATE.` → `SLOW CIRCLES. A BELL.` → `THEN IT COMES TO THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Arti. The waving of a lamp; the offering of light. It often closes a puja, the word from day eight: after the water and flowers and food, the lamp is circled before the image of God, and a song is sung. One arti song begins: Om jai jagadish hare. Victory to you, lord of the world. There's a line in the Katha Upanishad that helps with what the lamp might mean. The sun doesn't shine there, it says, nor the moon and stars, nor lightning, let alone this little fire. Then: tam eva bhantam anubhati sarvam. Everything shines after that one shining; by its light all this is lit. So when a small flame is held up before God, some teachers read it as light offered back to where light comes from. It's a humble gift. The lamp knows where its shine came from. Then the flame leaves the shrine and goes out to the people. Each person draws its warmth toward their face, taking some of the blessing in. The same small fire touches every face in the room. Nobody gets more of it. Nobody needs to. That's the picture in today's line: light passed hand to hand. That may be part of the pull of the evening arti. The day is going dark, and people make a small light on purpose, together, and share it.
screen: `ARTI — THE OFFERING OF LIGHT` · `EVERYTHING SHINES AFTER THAT ONE` · `LIGHT OFFERED BACK TO ITS SOURCE` · `THE SAME FIRE TOUCHES EVERY FACE` · then, large: `LIGHT PASSED HAND TO HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take the light, and pass it on. If there's a candle or a lamp near you, light it; if not, any light in the room will do. Look at it for a breath. Then cup your hands toward it, as if gathering warmth, and bring them to your eyes and forehead. Now bring one person to mind, near or far, and turn your cupped hands toward them, as if passing the plate. Then sit with the light. The bell holds the time.
Arti. The offering of light, and then the light shared with everyone. Fourteenth word. Puja, karma, atman, Brahman, guru, japa, arti: that's week two.
Your line: light passed hand to hand. Tonight, as it gets dark: one small light, one breath, one person you send it to. Next week brings the doing words. Day fourteen.

howItsDone: Arti is performed in temples and homes, often in the morning and evening: a lamp is waved before the image of God while a bell rings and a song is sung, and then the flame is brought to each person, who passes their hands over it and touches their eyes and forehead.

notes: Editor pass (days 8–14): 'it's why the evening arti has its own pull' softened to 'that may be part of the pull'; the practice's 'if you pray' line replaced so the week's practice closes don't repeat.

Written from the camp-one manuscript day 14 under the claims rule and the neighbor rule: the manuscript's list of other traditions' evening rites (Jewish candles, an Islamic prayer, vespers), 'every tradition noticed', the Varanasi reference and 'that's why Infinite Hill sits at sunset' were cut.

Katha 2.2.15 (5.15 in some numberings): na tatra suryo bhati na chandra-tarakam nema vidyuto bhanti kuto 'yam agnih / tam eva bhantam anubhati sarvam tasya bhasa sarvam idam vibhati. Paraphrased in English; transliteration quoted. Confirm.
'Some teachers read it as light offered back to where light comes from' links arti to this verse as an interpretation, not a textual claim. Confirm it's acceptable.

'Om jai jagadish hare' glossed as 'victory to you, lord of the world' (hare as a vocative of Hari); confirm the gloss. The song is commonly attributed to Shardha Ram Phillauri (nineteenth century); attribution left out of the voice.
Week two look-back in the word segment lists the seven words of days 8 to 14; the carry points to week three's 'doing words' as the manuscript does.
Audit (2026-10-01): cut the filler line 'then comes the second half, which carries its own meaning'. Katha 2.2.15 transliteration and the Om jai jagadish hare gloss checked; no factual errors found.
